title: Periyāzhwār and Āṇḍāḷ
body:
The story of Periyāzhwār begins with the story of Srivilliputtūr, the town from which he came.

In the southern Pāṇḍya kingdom there was a small town called Puttūr, where great scholars and paṇḍits lived. Beside it lay a forest inhabited by hunters, whose chief had two sons, Villi and Kaṇḍan. One day the two brothers went into the forest to hunt, as they always did. They spotted a tiger, but it escaped their arrows. Kaṇḍan gave chase and plunged deep into the forest, until the tiger, hiding behind a tree, sprang upon him and killed him. Villi waited long for his brother, then went searching for him, anxious for the brother he loved so dearly. When at last he found Kaṇḍan's body, his heart nearly stopped with grief; he wept bitterly and fell unconscious upon his brother.

As he lay unconscious, a vision rose before him. Sriman Nārāyaṇa appeared with His consort Mahālakshmi and, opening His coral lips, said: "O Villi, do not grieve or weep. We will restore your brother's life. Go together and find the great banyan tree in the midst of this forest, beneath which My form has lain for a long time. Near the tree you will find a cave filled with golden jewels, coins and treasure. Take as much as you need, and with that wealth clear the forest and build a temple and a town around it." Then the Lord vanished.

When Villi regained consciousness, he did not know whether what he had seen was true, and he was bewildered. But suddenly Kaṇḍan rose, alive and unhurt, as though waking from sleep. Villi told his brother all that had happened, and the two embraced, overjoyed that they had been blessed by the Lord and chosen by Him to establish a temple for Śriyaḥ Pati, the Lord of Śrī.

Vishṇuchittar

Scholars, devotees and paṇḍits moved from Puttūr to this holy place and made it their home. Among them was Mukunda Bhaṭṭar, a Vaishṇava jñāni, and his wife Padmavalli, a woman of every virtue and a perfect match for him. Both were devoted to Vaṭapatraśāyī, the Lord who reclines upon the banyan leaf. On an auspicious day a son was born to them, and they named him Vishṇuchittar, "the one whose mind dwells always on Vishṇu."

The child lived up to his name in every way, always contemplating how he might win the Lord's grace. Rather than spend his time on the study of the Vedas and Śāstras, he devoted himself wholly to praising the Lord. He knew that when Lord Kṛshṇa walked the earth, He loved to wear garlands of many flowers, and so he chose this as his kainkaryam: to pluck flowers early each morning and weave them into exquisite garlands for Sri Vaṭapatraśāyī. He even sold some of his property and bought a small plot near his home and the temple, which he turned into a beautiful nandavanam. There he grew every kind of flowering plant and creeper, and the sacred tulasī. The garden also held a small pond whose water was as clear as crystal and as pure as Vishṇuchittar's own heart.

He gave all his time to tending this garden and making it ever more beautiful, so that it would yield more and more flowers for the Lord. The flowers bloomed, the tulasī grew tall, and the whole garden became divinely beautiful, filled with the fragrance of jasmine, rose, lotus, pārijātam, alli and tulasī. Every morning before sunrise, Vishṇuchittar bathed, completed his daily observances, went to his garden, gathered flowers of every kind and wove garlands for the Lord, singing His praise all the while. He took them to the temple and delighted in seeing the Lord adorned with them, and this gave him boundless joy. He was blessed, too, with a wife who shared his love for serving the Lord.

Before the King's Court

Around the ninth century, the region was ruled from Madurai by a king named Vallabhadēvan. He was a good king who ruled wisely and was devoted to Sriman Nārāyaṇa, and he longed to understand the meaning of the Vedas and the nature of the Supreme Truth. He asked his chief minister how he might pursue this desire. The minister replied: "Let us invite Vedic scholars to answer your questions. Whoever answers well and resolves your doubts may be richly rewarded, O king." The king agreed, and it was proclaimed throughout the land. It was also announced that a bag of gold coins would hang high in the court, and that by the power and truth of the Vedic principle it would fall of its own accord when that principle was truly stated.

Many scholars and paṇḍits came, and there were debates, discourses and recitations, but the bag remained hanging. No one had stated the true principle underlying the Vedas, and the king was deeply disappointed.

Then the Lord began His play. Sri Vaṭapatraśāyī appeared in Vishṇuchittar's dream and said: "O devotee, I am pleased with your service of garlands. Tomorrow go to the palace, speak on the principles of the Vedas, and claim the reward." Vishṇuchittar replied: "I am not learned in the Vedas. I never even studied them. All I know is how to make a simple garland for You, Lord. I cannot speak of Vedic truths, for I do not know them." The Lord smiled. "O Vishṇuchitta, you are only an instrument. We will speak through you. Do not worry. Simply go."

The Lord also appeared in the chief minister's dream and asked him to bring Vishṇuchittar to the palace the next day in a palanquin, with full honours. The next day Vishṇuchittar prayed to the Lord, boarded the palanquin, and was carried to the palace with every honour. The scholars laughed at what they took to be his greed, knowing how little he knew of the Vedas, and made scornful remarks aloud. But once Vishṇuchittar, after a short prayer, began to speak, the murmurs died away, the scorn vanished, and everyone listened intently.

The king, the ministers, the people and the scholars could all follow his simple words, which were full of deep meaning and flowed like waves from a great ocean. Everyone understood him clearly, and when Vishṇuchittar concluded that Sri Mahāvishṇu, Śriyaḥ Pati, alone is the Paramporuḷ, the Supreme Being who protects and blesses the whole universe and all beings, and the one principle underlying all four Vedas, the bag fell of its own accord, straight into his hands.

The king rose at once, tears in his eyes, and prostrated at Vishṇuchittar's feet. "Now I am clear," he said. "You have resolved all my doubts. Sriman Nārāyaṇa alone is the Supreme. I have never heard such deep truths explained so simply." The scholars bowed their heads in shame, set aside their pride, and joined in celebrating Vishṇuchittar's victory. The king gave him still more gifts and honoured him with the title Bhaṭṭarpirān.

Vishṇuchittar, deeply moved and trembling at the Lord's mercy towards one so humble, replied: "O king, I am but a mute. I never spoke; it was He who spoke through me. He is the flute player; I am only the bamboo. I am only the plant; it is He who made the flower bloom. I am only a puppet; He is the doer and the puppeteer. Do not praise me, and do not bow at my feet. Let us all bow at His feet."

Pallāṇḍu

The king seated Vishṇuchittar upon the royal elephant and led a grand procession through the streets of the kingdom. People thronged everywhere to see the blessed soul, crying "Bhaṭṭarpirān vāzhga!" Vishṇuchittar wept tears of joy throughout, his palms joined, his mind wholly fixed on the Lord and His mercy.

The Lord Himself could not remain reclining on the Ocean of Milk while such a scene unfolded. He too wished to see His devotee honoured and praised. He appeared in the sky upon Garuḍa with Mahālakshmi, and the whole gathering, the king, the ministers, the people, and even the jealous scholars, beheld Him and His consort upon Garuḍa.

Seeing the Lord, Vishṇuchittar was ecstatic. Using the bells that hung from the elephant to keep the rhythm, he sang:

"Pallāṇḍu, pallāṇḍu, pallāyiraththāṇḍu, pala kōḍi nūrāyiram."

"Many years, many years, many thousands of years, many crores of hundreds of thousands of years."

He was blessing the Lord Himself, wishing that He might live on forever. That is why he is called Periyāzhwār, the elder Āzhwār: for he sought to protect and bless the Lord Himself.

Having received the title Bhaṭṭarpirān, Periyāzhwār continued his service of garlands, and sang Pāsurams on Kaṇṇan. He sang as though he had become the Lord's own mother, Yaśodā: bathing Him, feeding Him, dressing Him and playing with Him, imagining and delighting in every sweet trouble that Yaśodā had known. The Child's beauty, His mischief and His līlās are all sung by Periyāzhwār, and his Pāsurams are to be read, read again, and cherished.

Kōdhai

One day, on Āḍi Pūram, as he was gathering flowers and tulasī leaves in his garden, Periyāzhwār heard the faint cry of a baby. She was an incarnation of Bhūmi Dēvī. Delighted to find a tiny girl with beautiful limbs and a radiant golden face, he lifted her lovingly in both arms and covered her with kisses. When he and his wife held her, they felt as though they were holding Bāla Kṛshṇa Himself. They raised the child with boundless joy, and named her Kōdhai.

Surrounded by their love, their devotion, Pāsurams steeped in bhakti, and their service to the Lord, Kōdhai grew up with an immense love for Kaṇṇan. This was hardly surprising, for Kaṇṇan Himself had been brought up in that same house through Periyāzhwār's Pāsurams. Kōdhai grew into a girl of captivating beauty, with keen intelligence and deep knowledge of the Lord. Helping her father in his service, she grew ever closer to Kaṇṇan. She too plucked flowers and wove garlands with her father, and her words and thoughts were always of Kaṇṇan. She went with her father to the temple of Vaṭapatraśāyī with the garlands, to have the Lord's darśanam.

The years passed, and as Kōdhai grew, her devotion to Kaṇṇan grew beyond measure. She longed to see Him and be blessed by Him. Her love for Him was so great that she wished to marry Him, and vowed that she would marry no one else. She even dreamt of Him coming to her like a majestic elephant, clad in silk and pītāmbaram, for their wedding. She spent her days in such dreams, of Senkaṇ Tirumāl, the lotus-eyed Lord, taking her hand and walking around the sacred fire with her. Seeing all this, Periyāzhwār grew anxious about how his beloved daughter's wish could ever be fulfilled, when it seemed impossible for anyone to marry the Lord.

The Garland Worn First

One day, Periyāzhwār prepared the garlands of flowers and tulasī as usual, set them in a clean, safe place, and went out. Kōdhai, seeing such beautiful garlands, thought for a moment: "If I am to marry Him alone, why should I not wear these garlands before He does?" And she put them on. She wore them one by one, admiring her reflection in a mirror. Hearing footsteps, she quickly removed them and put them back.

When Periyāzhwār adorned the Lord with those garlands, the Lord looked exquisitely beautiful that day, and there was even a smile on His lips. The garlands filled the temple with a wonderful fragrance, and everyone spoke of how special they were. Periyāzhwār could not understand why that day was different, when he had done nothing out of the ordinary. They were the same flowers, the same tulasī, prepared in the same way. Why, then, such fragrance and such beauty? He did not know.

This went on day after day. Kōdhai secretly wore the garlands and admired herself in them, and the Lord wore them with great joy and contentment, and they shed a wonderful fragrance. No one knew why.

Then, one day, on Kṛshṇa Jayanti, Periyāzhwār saw Kōdhai wearing the garland. He was deeply angry and distressed, hurt and full of sorrow, and he asked her: "Kōdhai, my child, why have you committed such a great sin? Was this not meant for the Lord, Sriman Nārāyaṇa? How could you make it impure by wearing it yourself?"

Kōdhai replied with regret, and yet with conviction: "Father, Sriman Nārāyaṇa is in my heart, and I wished to see Him wearing them. Will the Lord be angry if His devotee wears them first?"

Her eyes filled with tears of guilt, and Periyāzhwār's heart melted to see his darling child cry. He held her gently and consoled her: "It is not that, Kōdhai. This is meant for our Lord. Does it not become impure when we wear it, my dear one? Never mind. Do not worry. Only do not do it again. Today I will make another garland; let this one be set aside. Do not cry."

He made a fresh garland and adorned the Lord with it, but that day there was no fragrance, no beauty and no radiance on the Lord's face, and no smile on His lips. The archakas too were puzzled.

Periyāzhwār was saddened that he had been angry with his sweet child for the first time, and that the Lord had not looked radiant in the second garland. He slept restlessly, and just before dawn, Gōvinda appeared in his dream. Opening His beautiful coral lips, He said: "My dearest Vishṇuchitta, Periyāzhwār, Bhaṭṭarpirān! Kōdhai was born as your daughter to sing her pāmālai, her garlands of verse, and to wear My pūmālai, My garlands of flowers, and it is the garlands she has worn that I love to wear. She has ruled over Me with her garlands of verse and of flowers, and so from now on she shall be called Āṇḍāḷ, the one who rules. Do not stop her from wearing the garlands. Let her continue."

Periyāzhwār woke and understood Kōdhai's greatness. Thrilled to know that she was the one who ruled the Lord, he called her Āṇḍāḷ, and he told her everything. Āṇḍāḷ's face flushed with shyness. She came to be known far and wide as Sūḍikkoḍutta Suḍarkkoḍi, "the radiant maiden who gave to the Lord the garland she had worn."

Āṇḍāḷ at Srirangam

Āṇḍāḷ composed the Tiruppāvai, thirty verses, as a means of performing prapatti, surrender, to the Lord and seeking refuge at His lotus feet. The great teachers who came after her recognised the profound depths of this composition.

When Periyāzhwār raised the subject of marriage, Kōdhai would name no groom but Gōvinda. Periyāzhwār understood her well, for he himself had raised her to think of nothing but Kaṇṇan. He knew, too, that it was Sri Ranganātha who had stolen her heart. He worried, rightly, how she could possibly be married to the Almighty, and his worry grew day by day, just as Āṇḍāḷ's love for the Lord grew.

The Lord appeared in Periyāzhwār's dream and asked him to come to Srirangam the next day. He also appeared in the dream of the Pāṇḍya king Vallabhan and asked him to bring Āṇḍāḷ and Periyāzhwār to Srirangam with full honours. The next day the king and his retinue, the archakas of the Srirangam temple, his officers and ministers, and all the people of Srivilliputtūr gathered at Periyāzhwār's house. Palanquin, ceremonial umbrella, fly-whisks, the temple elephant and the royal elephant were all brought to carry the blessed father and daughter. The women adorned the already lovely Āṇḍāḷ in silk, gold and jewels.

Periyāzhwār and Vallabhan led Kōdhai slowly and lovingly to the palanquin, and Āṇḍāḷ took her seat in it with the grace of a bride. All along the way there were arches of flowers and festive decorations, and crowds thronged to see the blessed beauty of Srivilliputtūr. They reached Srirangam and were led straight to the sanctum, the sannidhi of Tiruvarangan. Kōdhai stepped into the inner court, gazed upon the Lord's face, and at once merged with Him as a jyoti, a divine light.

Periyāzhwār was overcome with grief and wept bitterly at the loss of his beloved daughter to the Lord. Though he knew the whole of bhakti and the meaning of the Vedas, he could not hold back his tears at being parted from his dearest Kōdhai:

"Oru magaḷai uḍaiyēn; ulagam niraindha pugazhāl
tirumagaḷ pōl vaḷarththēn; sengaṇmāl thān koṇḍu pōnān."

"I had but one daughter. I raised her like Tirumagaḷ, Mahālakshmi Herself, and her fame filled the world. Now the red lotus-eyed Lord has taken her away."

Periyāzhwār felt suddenly old after losing his child. With the king's help he consecrated a vigraham of Āṇḍāḷ in Srivilliputtūr, and until his last day he continued his service of garlands to Sri Vaṭapatraśāyī, with a heavy heart and his thoughts always on Kōdhai.

"Pāthagangaḷ thīrkkum, paraman aḍi kāṭṭum,
vēdham anaiththukkum viththāgum, kōdhai thamizh;
aiyaindhum aindhum ariyādha mānidarai
vaiyam sumappadhum vambu."

"It removes all our sins and reveals the feet of the Supreme; it is the seed of all the Vedas. That is Kōdhai's Tamizh. Those who do not know these thirty verses are only a burden to the earth."

To recite these thirty verses of the Tiruppāvai each morning is to seek the blessing of Āṇḍāḷ, who is none other than Bhūmi Pirāṭṭi, and whose grace alone can free us from the sorrows of samsāra.
